Typhoon Haiyan also known as Yolanda was the strongest typhoon in the Philippines.

Diwata-1 also known as PHL-Microsat-1 is a Philippine microsatellite launched to the International Space Station (ISS) on March 23, 2016, and was deployed into orbit from the ISS on April 27, 2016. It is the first Philippine microsatellite and the first satellite built and designed by Filipinos.
Rodrigo Duterte, the 16th President of the Philippines.
The Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled in favor of the Philippines against China over territorial disputes in the South China Sea.
A building in Marawi is set ablaze by air strikes carried out by the Philippine Air Force.

April – The High Court rules that same-sex marriage is legal.
Mines and Energy Minister Ernest Kabushemeye was eaten by cannibals in Bujumbura.
They later sign peace agreements with seven other ethnic groups.
Resistance of Honorius cousins in Spain. Constantine III sends his son Constans II with an army.
Gerontius, Roman general (magister militum) ends the revolt in Hispain.
Gerontius, who had been a partisan of Constantine III, revolts in Hispania. He elevates Maximus, his domesticus, as emperor.

The Vandals, led by King Gunderic, cross the Pyrenees into the Iberian Peninsula. They receive land from the Romans, as foederati, in Baetica (Southern Spain). The Alans occupy lands in Lusitania and the Suebi control parts of Gallaecia.
Gerontius successfully defended himself against Constans II.
The Alans establish their rule in the Roman province of Lusitania (Portugal south of the Duero River and Spain).
Wallia is campaigning against the Vandals and Alans on behalf of Emperor Honorius.
Emperor Honorius bribes Wallia, king of the Visigoths, into regaining Hispania for the Roman Empire. His victory over the Vandals forces them to retire to Baetica.
Comes Asterius conducts campaign in Gallaecia and ends the usurpation of Maximus. A Roman army under command of vicar Maurocellus suffers a defeat at Braga in Gallaecia.
Vandal war: The Roman commander-in-chief Castinus leads a defeat against the Vandals at Baetica.
The Vandals including Alans, led by Genseric ("Caesar King"), cross the narrow Strait of Gibraltar with their families from the Iberian Peninsula.
Rechila conquers the city Mérida.
Rechila invades Baetica and conquers the capital Seville
the Gothic king Theoderic II starts a war commissioned by the West Roman emperor Avitus.
The fleet Emperor Majorian assembles in Nova Carthago (Cartagena) in preparation for an invasion of the Vandal Kingdom in Africa becomes destroyed by the Vandal king Geiseric.
The Suevic nation in Galicia (Northern Spain) is unified under King Remismund.
The Gothic king Euric orders his army to conquer the province of Tarragonenses.
The comes Hispaniarum Vincentius capitulates against the Aquitanian Goths. The Goths complete their conquest of Spain.

The Franks attacked allied with the Burgundians to the Visigothic Kingdom of Toulouse. Alaric II was killed at the Battle of Vouillé, and Toulouse was sacked. The Visigoths had lost most of their Gallic holdings and are retreated to Hispania and Septimania, helped by Ostrogoths. Kingdom of Toulouse ended and The Arian Kingdom of Hispania began. Barcelona was the new capital of the Visigoths. From this moment, little by little, Visigothic Hispania will be the first effective realisation of an independent Kingdom or State of wholly Hispanic territories and scope.
Byzantine Empire conquered part of the south of the Visigothic kingdom.
Toledo. Capital of the Visigothic kingdom by the end of the reign of Athanagild.

Liuvigild began his reign. He is among the greatest Visigothic kings of the Arian period because he consolidated Visigothic power in Spain. He is known for his Code of Leovigild, a law that allowed equal rights between the Visigothic and Hispano-Roman populations, and for expanding the territory of the Visigothic Kingdom. Since Leovigild, the Visigoth kings minted their own Tremissis coin.
Liuvigild conquered the Suebic Kingdom.
The Third Council of Toledo marks the entry of Visigothic Spain into the Catholic Church, after Reccared I converted in 587. The Catholic Kingdom of Toledo began.
Swinthila reconquered the south of Byzantine Hispania.

"History of the Kings of the Goths" is written by Isidore of Seville. In the prologue, "Laus Spaniae" (Praises to Spain), introduces the phrase mater Spania (mother Spain) and defends the Gothic identity of a unified Spain.
The entire Hispania and Septimania is under the Visigothic Kingdom. Swinthila defeated the Basques.
Recceswinth was responsible for the promulgation of a law code, Liber Iudiciorum. The new laws applied to both Gothic and Hispano-Roman populations.
The Battle of Guadalete was the first major battle of the Umayyad conquest of Hispania. Roderic, the last Visigoth king in Hispania under the rule from Toledo, died in the battle.
The Visigothic nobleman Pelagius of Asturias rebelled against the Umayyad Caliphate.
Battle of Covadonga: Forces loyal to Pelagius decimated an Umayyad army sent to reconquer them in a valley in the Picos de Europa.
Pelagius was elected princeps of the independent Kingdom of Asturias with his capital at Cangas de Onís.
Pelagius died. He was succeeded as princeps by his son Favila of Asturias.
Favila was killed by a bear while hunting. He was succeeded by his brother-in-law Alfonso I the Catholic of Asturias, the son of Peter of Cantabria, the duke of Cantabria.
Asturias conquered and annexed Galicia.
Alfonso the Catholic died. He was succeeded as king by his son Fruela I the Cruel of Asturias.
Fruela was assassinated.
Fruela's cousin Aurelius of Asturias was crowned king of Asturias.
Aurelius died. He was succeeded by his cousin-in-law, Silo of Asturias, husband of Alfonso the Catholic's daughter Adosinda. Silo established his capital at Pravia.
Silo died.
Adosinda engineered the election of her nephew Alfonso II the Chaste of Asturias, son of Fruela, as king of Asturias.
A coalition of nobles elected Alfonso the Catholic's illegitimate son Mauregatus of Asturias king of Asturias. Alfonso the Chaste fled to Álava.
Mauregatus died.
Aurelius's brother Bermudo I the Deacon, the Monk of Asturias was elected king of Asturias.
Battle of the Burbia River: An Asturian force attacked a Cordoban army near Villafranca del Bierzo on its return to Córdoba and was defeated.
Bermudo abdicated the throne.
Alfonso the Chaste was crowned king of Asturias in Oviedo, Spain.
Alfonso the Chaste established his capital at Oviedo.
Battle of Lutos: A Cordoban army returning from a scorched earth campaign in modern Álava was wiped out by an Asturian force.
Battle of Las Babias: Córdoba attacked and routed an Asturian force near Astorga, Spain.
Battle of Pancorbo (816): Córdoba slaughtered a Basque-Asturian force defending the Basque homeland in the Pyrenees at Pancorbo.

Battle of Roncevaux Pass (824): A combined force of Basques and the Banu Qasi, both vassals of the emirate of Córdoba, defeated a Carolingian military expedition in the Roncevaux Pass. The Basque chieftain Íñigo Arista of Pamplona was crowned king of Navarre at Pamplona.
Alfonso the Chaste died.
The Asturian nobility elected Nepotian of Asturias, a relative of Alfonso the Chaste, king.
Battle of the Bridge of Cornellana: Forces loyal to Bermudo's son Ramiro I of Asturias defeated Nepotian in modern Salas, Asturias.
Ramiro died. He was buried in the Pantheon of Asturian Kings in Oviedo. His son Ordoño I of Asturias succeeded him as king.
Battle of Albelda (851): Ordoño suppressed a Basque revolt in northeastern Asturias and expelled an opportunistic Cordoban invasion near Albelda.
Íñigo died. He was succeeded as king of Navarre by his son García Íñiguez of Pamplona.
Battle of Guadalacete: Asturian and Pamplonan forces arriving in support of a revolt of the people of Toledo, Spain were routed by a Cordoban army.
Vikings captured García and extorted a ransom of some seventy thousand gold dinars from Navarre for his return.
Cordoban forces captured García's son and heir Fortún Garcés the One-Eyed, the Monk of Pamplona in Milagro, Navarre.
An eastern march of Asturias was created the county of Castile under count Rodrigo of Castile.
Battle of the Morcuera: Córdoba attacked Asturias, forcing the retreat of Asturian forces and their Castilian allies along the valley of the Ebro.
Ordoño died. He was succeeded by his eldest son Alfonso III the Great of Asturias.
Fruela seized the throne of Asturias and forced Alfonso the Great to flee to Castile.
Fruela was assassinated in Oviedo.
Asturias conquered Porto. Vímara Peres was created count of Portugal.
García died. García Jiménez of Pamplona took power as regent, García's son and heir Fortún Garcés remaining in captivity in Córdoba.
Rodrigo died. He was succeeded as count of Castile by his son Diego Rodríguez Porcelos.
Asturias conquered Coimbra.
First Battle of Cellorigo: Vela Jiménez, count of the Asturian county of Álava, repelled an attempted conquest by the Emirate of Córdoba of an important mountain pass at Cellorigo.
Fortún Garcés was returned to rule in Navarre.
Second Battle of Cellorigo: Vela Jiménez repelled an attempted conquest by the Emirate of Córdoba of an important mountain pass at Cellorigo.
Rodríguez died.
Day of Zamora: The Asturian defenders of Zamora, Spain dealt heavy casualties to a Cordoban force attempting to conquer it. The heads of the besiegers were displayed on the city walls.
The Navarrese nobility removed Fortún Garcés from the throne, placing Sancho I of Pamplona there in his stead.

Alfonso the Great died and was buried at Oviedo Cathedral. His kingdom was divided among his three sons, with his eldest, García I of León, receiving León, Ordoño II of León receiving Galicia, and Fruela II of Asturias receiving a rump Asturias including Castile.
García I died. His lands passed to Ordoño II.
Battle of San Esteban de Gormaz (917): Leonese forces broke a Cordoban siege of San Esteban de Gormaz.

Battle of Valdejunquera: A Cordoban army invading Castile routed a joint Leonese-Navarrese force at Valdejunquera, probably between modern Estella-Lizarra and Pamplona, forcing the abandonment by León of Clunia.
Navarre defeated Galindo Aznárez II, count of the County of Aragon, in battle and forced him into vassalage.
Ordoño II died.
The Leonese nobility elected Fruela II king of León.

Fruela II died, possibly from leprosy. His will named his son Alfonso Fróilaz his successor. Ordoño II's sons Sancho Ordóñez, Alfonso IV the Monk of León and Ramiro II of León did not recognize Fróilaz's succession, however, leaving him in de facto authority only in Galicia.
Fruela II's younger brother, a Ramiro, married his widow Urraca bint Abd Allah and claimed the royal title.
Ordóñez, Alfonso the Monk and Ramiro II forced Fróilaz into exile in the eastern marches of Asturias.
Ordóñez seized León, Spain.
Alfonso the Monk, with the support of Navarre and the Leonese nobility, expelled Ordóñez from León, Spain.
Sancho I died. He was succeeded by his young son García Sánchez I of Pamplona with his brother Jimeno Garcés of Pamplona acting as regent.
Ordóñez was crowned princeps of Galicia.
Ordóñez died. His territory passed to Alfonso the Monk.
Fernán González of Castile became count of Castile.
Álvaro Herraméliz, count of Lantarón and Álava, died. Fernán González inherited his territories and united them with Castile.
Jimeno Garcés died.
Alfonso the Monk was forced to abdicate the rule of León and Galicia to his brother Ramiro II.
Battle of Simancas: A battle began near Simancas which would see a joint Leonese-Navarrese force repel an attempted Cordoban conquest of the lands around the Douro.
Battle of Alhandic: Cordoban forces conquered the Leonese city of Zamora, Spain with great cost in lives to both sides.
Ramiro II died and was buried in the Basílica de San Isidoro, León. He was succeeded by his son Ordoño III of León.
Ordoño III died in Zamora, Spain. He was succeeded by his half-brother Sancho I the Fat of León.
The Leonese nobility, led by Fernán González, deposed Sancho the Fat in favor of Alfonso the Monk's son Ordoño IV the Wicked, the Bad of León.
Sancho the Fat was restored to the throne of León with the support of Navarre and Córdoba.

Sancho the Fat was poisoned by count Gonzalo Menéndez of Portugal and buried in the Basílica de San Isidoro, León. He was succeeded by his young son Ramiro III of León, with the latter's aunt Elvira Ramírez and mother Teresa Ansúrez ruling as regents.
García Sánchez I died. He was succeeded by his eldest son Sancho II of Pamplona. A small territory around Viguera he willed to another son as the Kingdom of Viguera.
Fernán González died. He was succeeded as count of Castile by his son García Fernández of the White Hands of Castile.
Battle of Torrevicente: A Cordoban force dealt a bloody defeat to a rebel Cordoban general and his Vigueran and Castilian allies, probably near Atienza.
Battle of Rueda: A Cordoban force dealt a decisive defeat to a joint Leonese-Navarrese army in Rueda, Valladolid.
The Galician nobility acclaimed Ordoño III's son Bermudo II the Gouty of León king of Galicia with the support of the Caliphate of Córdoba.
Bermudo deposed Ramiro III and replaced him as king of León.
León expelled Cordoban forces from Zamora, Spain.
The Leonese nobility expelled Bermudo from the kingdom.
Bermudo was allowed to return to León.
Sancho II died and was buried at San Juan de la Peña. He was succeeded as king of Navarre and count of Aragon by his son García Sánchez II of Pamplona.
Fernández was captured by a Cordoban raiding party.
Fernández died of his wounds at Medinaceli. He was succeeded by his son Sancho García of the Good Laws of Castile.
Córdoba conquered the Leonese city of Astorga, Spain.
Castile declined to pay its annual tribute to Córdoba.

Bermudo died. He was succeeded by his young son Alfonso V the Noble of León, with the latter's mother Elvira of Castile, Queen of León and the count Menendo González, count of Portugal and duke in Galicia, acting as regents.
Battle of Cervera: Córdoba defeated the combined forces of García of the Good Laws and García Gómez, count of Saldaña, Carrión and Liébana on a punitive expedition near modern Espinosa de Cervera.

García Sánchez II died. He was succeeded as king of Navarre and count of Aragon by his young son Sancho III the Great of Pamplona, with the latter's mother Jimena Fernández and grandmother Urraca Fernandez ruling with the bishops of Navarre as regents.
A Cordoban army under the caliph Hisham II invaded León with the intent of conquering Zamora, Spain.
García Ramírez of Viguera, king of Viguera, died without male heirs. His territory was absorbed by Navarre.
Menendo González died. Alfonso the Noble entered his majority.
Hisham was overthrown and imprisoned by his cousin Muhammad II of Córdoba.
Sulayman ibn al-Hakam, at the head of an army of disaffected Berbers and with the help of García of the Good Laws, defeated Muhammad, forcing the latter to flee to Toledo, Spain, and freed Hisham.
Sancho the Great married García of the Good Laws's daughter Muniadona of Castile.
Sancho the Great conquered the county of Sobrarbe.

García of the Good Laws died. He was succeeded as count of Castile and Álava by his young son García Sánchez of Castile, with Urraca of Covarrubias, the latter's aunt and Fernández's daughter, acting as regent with the Castilian nobility.
Sancho the Great annexed half of the county of Ribagorza.
Raymond III of Pallars Jussà, count of Pallars Jussà and the rump Ribagorza, pledged submission to Sancho the Great as his vassal.
Alfonso the Noble died. He was succeeded as king of León by his son Bermudo III of León.
García Sánchez was assassinated in León, Spain by the sons of a noble he had expelled from the lands between the Cea and the Pisuerga.
Sancho the Great appointed Ferdinand I the Great of León, his son and grandson of García of the Good Laws on his mother's side, count of Castile.
Hisham III of Córdoba, the caliph of Córdoba in exile, was overthrown and his title abolished by the local nobility, resulting in the immediate de jure independence of the taifas of Al-Andalus.
Alfonso the Noble's daughter Sancha of León was married to Ferdinand the Great.
Navarre conquered León, Spain. Bermudo III fled to modern Galicia.

Sancho the Great died. His kingdom was divided among his sons. Gonzalo of Sobrarbe and Ribagorza received Sobrarbe and Ribagorza. The illegitimate Ramiro I of Aragon was granted the title of bailiff and some property in Aragon. García Sánchez III of Pamplona succeeded his father as king of Navarre and held suzerainty over his brothers.
Battle of Tafalla: García Sánchez III repelled an invasion of his kingdom by Ramiro I.
Battle of Tamarón: Bermudo III of León fell from his horse and was slain by forces loyal to Ferdinand the Great.
Ferdinand the Great was crowned king of León and Castile in León, Spain.
Gonzalo of Sobrarbe and Ribagorza was assassinated by one of his knights.
Ramiro I annexed Sobrarbe and Ribagorza.

Battle of Atapuerca: Navarrese and Leonese forces met near modern Atapuerca, Province of Burgos. García Sánchez III and his tutor Fortún Sánchez were killed. García Sánchez III's son Sancho IV of Peñalén of Pamplona succeeded him as king under the regency of Stephanie, Queen of Navarre. León annexed Navarrese territories south of the Ebro.
Ferdinand the Great crowned himself Imperator totius Hispaniae.
Stephanie died.
Sancho of Peñalén and Ferdinand the Great signed a treaty defining their border.
Synod of Jaca (1063): Ramiro I presided over a synod in Jaca which reestablished the Roman Catholic Diocese of Huesca.
Battle of Graus: Ramiro I died in a failed attempt to take Graus from the taifa of Zaragoza. He was succeeded by his son Sancho Ramírez.
Crusade of Barbastro: At the urging of the pope Pope Alexander II, a coalition of Aragon, Urgell, Aquitaine and the Papal States conquered Barbastro from the taifa of Lérida.
Battle of Paterna: Valencian forces pursuing the army of Ferdinand the Great, then in retreat from a failed siege of Valencia, were ambushed and wiped out at Paterna.

Ferdinand the Great died. His kingdom was divided among his three children. The eldest, Sancho II the Strong of Castile and León, received Castile. León was divided; Galicia went to García II of Galicia, and the remainder went to Alfonso VI the Brave, the Valiant of León and Castile.
War of the Three Sanchos: Sancho the Strong began ordering border raids on Navarre.
War of the Three Sanchos: The war reached a stalemate. Castile remained in possession of the Navarrese territories in modern Álava, Montes de Oca, Pancorbo, Burgos and La Rioja.
Alfonso the Brave invaded the taifa of Badajoz.
Battle of Llantada: Sancho the Strong defeated Alfonso the Brave at Llantadilla, in the taifa of Badajoz near modern Melgar de Fernamental.
Sancho the Strong and Alfonso the Brave invaded Galicia from the north and south, respectively, partitioning the kingdom and forcing García II into exile in Seville.
Battle of Golpejera: Sancho the Strong defeated and captured Alfonso the Brave near Carrión de los Condes. The latter was released and sent into exile in Toledo.
Sancho the Strong was crowned king of León.
Sancho the Strong was betrayed and murdered by a Zamoran noble during his assault on Zamora, Spain.
Alfonso the Brave succeeded his brother Sancho the Strong as king of León and Castile.
The taifas of Toledo and Granada were forced to pay the parias to Alfonso the Brave.
Sancho of Peñalén was thrown from a cliff in Peñalén by his brother and sister. Alfonso the Brave recognized his young son García Sánchez as his successor.
The Navarrese nobility elected Sancho Ramírez king. The latter ceded some territory in Navarre's west to Alfonso the Brave.
The Emir of Zaragoza began to pay the parias to Alfonso the Brave.
Alfonso the Brave took the title Imperator totius Hispaniae.
Battle of Cabra: Seville defeated the invading forces of Granada. Both sides were aided by Castilian knights.
Alfonso the Brave conquered Coria, Cáceres.
Sancho Ramírez conquered Graus.
Under the pretense of surrender, the occupants of the castle of Rueda de Jalón, a Zaragozan stronghold, invited important nobles of León to the castle and murdered them.
Battle of Morella: A Zaragozan army led by the general El Cid decisively defeated the forces of Sancho Ramírez near Tortosa.
Battle of Piedra Pisada: A Zaragozan army skirmished with the forces of Alfonso the Brave, then following the valley of the Cinca from Naval, Huesca to El Grado.
Alfonso the Brave conquered Toledo, Spain.
Alfonso the Brave conquered modern Madrid.
Alfonso the Brave installed his vassal, an al-Qádir, as king of Valencia.

Battle of Sagrajas: Yusuf ibn Tashfin, the sultan of the Almoravid dynasty, at the head of a coalition of Andalusian taifas, defeated León and Castile and Aragon in a bloody battle near Badajoz. The taifas renounced payment of the parias.

Siege of Tudela: Alfonso the Brave, Sancho Ramírez, Odo I, Duke of Burgundy, the duke of Burgundy, and William the Carpenter, viscount of Melun, laid siege to the Zaragozan fortress at Tudela, Navarre.
Sancho Ramírez conquered Estada.
Sancho Ramírez took the Castle of Montearagón.
Sancho Ramírez conquered Monzón.
Yusuf overthrew the king of Valencia and sent him into exile.
Sancho Ramírez died during a siege of Huesca. He was succeeded as king of Aragon and Navarre by his eldest son Peter I of Aragon and Pamplona.
El Cid reconquered Valencia, Spain for Castile.
Alfonso the Brave lost Lisbon, Sintra and Santarém, Portugal to Almoravid conquests.
The pope Pope Urban II issued a bull forbidding the excommunication of Peter I or his queen Agnes of Aquitaine, Queen of Aragon and Navarre without his express authorization.
Battle of Alcoraz: Peter I defeated the Zaragozan forces sent to relieve his siege of Huesca.
Peter I conquered Huesca.
Battle of Bairén: An Aragonese army pinned between Almoravid forces and the Mediterranean Sea routed their enemies near modern Gandia.
Battle of Consuegra: An Almoravid force defeated one of Alfonso the Brave's armies near Consuegra.
Peter I married Bertha of Aragon in Huesca, marking the transfer of the Aragonese capital from Jaca.
Alfonso the Brave ordered Valencia evacuated and burned in the face of an Almoravid threat.
Alfonso the Brave conquered the Almoravid city of Medinaceli.
Peter I died. He was succeeded as king of Aragon and Navarre by his brother Alfonso I the Battler of Aragon.
Alfonso the Battler conquered the Almoravid cities of Ejea de los Caballeros and Tauste.
Alfonso the Battler conquered Tamarite de Litera and San Esteban de Litera from the Almoravid dynasty.

Battle of Uclés (1108): The Almoravids dealt a decisive defeat to the forces of Alfonso the Brave at Uclés, reconquering the city as well as Cuenca, Spain, Huete and Ocaña, Spain. Alfonso the Brave's son and heir Sancho Alfónsez was killed in flight by local Muslims.
Alfonso the Brave died in Toledo, Spain. His daughter Urraca the Restless of León succeeded him as queen regnant of León and Castile.
Urraca the Restless married Alfonso the Battler.
Battle of Candespina: Alfonso the Battler, joined by Henry, Count of Portugal, the count of Portugal, defeated forces loyal to the former's wife Urraca the Restless at Fresno de Cantespino.

Battle of Viadangos: The noble Pedro Fróilaz de Traba and Diego Gelmírez, archbishop of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Santiago de Compostela, marching in support of Urraca the Restless, were routed at Villadangos del Páramo by a superior force led by Alfonso the Battler.
The pope Pope Paschal II annulled the marriage of Urraca the Restless to Alfonso the Battler. The two agreed to a truce.
Alfonso the Battler conquered the Almoravid cities of Fitero, Belchite, Corella, Spain, Cintruénigo, Murchante, Monteagudo, Navarre, and Cascante.
Alfonso the Battler, joined by French soldiers following the declaration of a crusade, conquered the Almoravid cities of Almudévar, Gurrea de Gállego and Zuera and laid siege to Zaragoza.
Alfonso the Battler conquered Zaragoza.
Alfonso the Battler conquered Cervera, Tudejen, Castellón, Tarazona, Ágreda, Magallón, Borja, Zaragoza, Alagón, Zaragoza, Novillas, Mallén, Rueda, Valladolid and Épila from the Almoravid dynasty.
Battle of Cutanda: Alfonso the Battler defeated forces of the Almoravid dynasty at Cutanda near Calamocha, conquering that town as well as Calatayud and Daroca for Aragon.
Alfonso the Battler conquered the Almoravid cities of Calatayud, Bubierca, Alhama de Aragón, Ariza, Zaragoza and Daroca.
Alfonso the Battler established the Confraternity of Belchite, a military order at Belchite devoted to war with Muslims.
Alfonso the Battler conquered the Barcelonan city of Lleida.

Urraca the Restless died in childbirth at Saldaña de Burgos. Alfonso VII the Emperor of León and Castile, her son by her first husband Raymond of Burgundy, succeeded her as king of Castile and León, though Alfonso the Battler remained in control of the former kingdom.
Alfonso the Battler conquered the Almoravid city of Longares.

Alfonso the Emperor and Alfonso the Battler signed the Peace of Támara at Támara de Campos. The treaty recognized Alfonso the Emperor's sovereignty over Castile and reestablished the 1054 border between Castile and Aragon. Alfonso the Battler renounced the title of emperor.
Afonso I the Conqueror of Portugal, the count of Portugal, took the title prince.
Siege of Bayonne: Alfonso the Battler laid siege to the Aquitainian city of Bayonne, probably with the intent of impressing Alfonso the Emperor's vassal Alfonso Jordan, the count of Toulouse.
Alfonso the Battler drafted a will leaving his kingdom to the Knights Templar, the Knights Hospitaller, and the Order of the Holy Sepulchre.
Siege of Bayonne: Alfonso the Battler withdrew after failing to conquer Bayonne.
Alfonso the Battler conquered the Almoravid city of Mequinenza.
Battle of Fraga: The Almoravids broke an Aragonese siege of Fraga. Alfonso the Battler was wounded.
Alfonso the Battler died of wounds suffered at the Battle of Fraga.
The Navarrese nobility elected García Ramírez of Navarre, a grandson of García Sánchez III's illegitimate son, king of Navarre.
The Aragonese nobility elected Ramiro II the Monk of Aragon king of Aragon.
Alfonso the Emperor took the title Imperator totius Hispaniae.

Ramiro the Monk's daughter Petronilla of Aragon was betrothed to Ramon Berenguer IV the Saint, Count of Barcelona, the count of Barcelona. Under the terms of the contract, Petronilla was appointed Ramiro the Monk's heir, and in the event of her childless death, Ramon Berenguer the Saint was to inherit all her territories.
Ramiro the Monk retired to the monastery, retaining the royal title but granting Ramon Berenguer the Saint royal authority under the title prince of the Aragonese people.
Siege of Coria (1138): Alfonso the Emperor failed to take the Almoravid city of Coria, Caceres. His commanding general Rodrigo Martínez was killed in the assault.
Siege of Oreja: Alfonso the Emperor laid siege to the Almoravid castle at Colmenar de Oreja.
Battle of Ourique: Afonso defeated an Almoravid force deep inside Almoravid territory at Ourique. His soldiers proclaimed him king of Portugal.
Siege of Oreja: The Almoravid garrison surrendered.
Battle of Valdevez: Afonso invaded Galicia. Alfonso the Emperor met him at Arcos de Valdevez and was defeated.
Siege of Coria (1142): Alfonso the Emperor laid siege to the Almoravid city of Coria, Caceres.
Siege of Coria (1142): The Almoravid garrison surrendered.
Afonso and Alfonso the Emperor signed the Treaty of Zamora in Zamora, Spain, under which the latter recognized the independence of Portugal and pledged peace between Portugal and León.

Second Crusade: Alfonso the Emperor, Ramon Berenguer the Saint and García Ramírez, with the support of the Genoese and Pisan navies, conquered the Almoravid port city of Almería. One-third of the city was granted to Genoa, the rest to Castile.
Alfonso the Emperor and Ramon Berenguer the Saint signed the Treaty of Tudilén, recognizing recent Aragonese conquests as well as any further conquests in the Taifa of Murcia.
The Almohad Caliphate conquered Almería.
Ramiro the Monk died. Petronilla succeeded him as queen regnant of Aragon.
Alfonso the Emperor died. His kingdom was divided between his two sons. The elder, Sancho III the Desired of Castile, received Castile; the younger, Ferdinand II of León, received León.
Sancho the Desired died. He was succeeded as king of Castile by his young son Alfonso VIII the Noble of Castile. A number of Castilian nobles began to vie for the regency.
Ramon Berenguer the Saint died. He was succeeded as count of Barcelona by his young son Alfonso II the Chaste, the Troubadour of Aragon.
Petronilla abdicated the throne of Aragon in favor of her young son Alfonso the Chaste.
Alfonso the Chaste conquered the county of Provence.
Alfonso the Chaste conquered Cerdanya.

Alfonso the Chaste and Sancho VI the Wise of Navarre, king of Navarre, signed the Treaty of Sangüesa providing for a twenty-year truce between their countries and agreeing to a division of the Taifa of Murcia.
Alfonso the Chaste conquered Teruel and Caspe.
Girard II of Roussillon, count of Roussillon, died without heirs. The nobles of his county elected Alfonso the Chaste to succeed him.
Alfonso the Chaste gifted Provence to his brother Ramon Berenguer III, Count of Provence.
Alfonso the Noble ceded Uclés to the Order of Santiago.
Castile conquered Cuenca, Spain.
Alfonso the Noble and Alfonso the Chaste signed the Treaty of Cazola, setting out their respective zones of conquest in Andalusia. Aragon ceded the right to Murcia.
Alfonso the Noble recognized Alfonso IX of León as king of León. In exchange, Alfonso IX recognized the supremacy of Castile over León.

Battle of Alarcos: The Almohad Caliphate decisively defeated a Castilian force in what is now the province of Ciudad Real, forcing the latter's retreat to Toledo, Spain and cession of Trujillo, Cáceres, Montánchez and Talavera de la Reina.
Alfonso the Chaste died. He was succeeded as king by his son Peter II the Catholic of Aragon.
Albigensian Crusade: The pope Pope Innocent III called for a crusade to exterminate Catharism in Languedoc.

Alfonso the Noble, Peter the Catholic, Sancho VII the Strong, the Prudent of Navarre, king of Navarre, and the papal legate Arnaud Amalric, at the head of an army of Franks, conquered the Almohad cities of Calatrava la Vieja, Alarcos and Benavente, Zamora.

Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa: A coalition of Castilian, Aragonese, Portuguese and Navarrese forces, joined by the Order of Santiago, the Order of Calatrava, the Knights Templar and French and Leonese volunteers, decisively defeated an Almohad army in what is now the Province of Jaén. The caliph Muhammad al-Nasir was forced into flight.

Battle of Muret: Peter the Catholic was killed in battle at Muret in an attempt to reinstall his vassal Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse, count of County of Toulouse. His army was routed. Peter the Catholic was succeeded by his young son James I the Conqueror of Aragon.
Alfonso the Noble died. He was succeeded by his young son Henry I of Castile, whose elder sister Berengaria of Castile ruled as regent.
Henry I was killed by a tile falling off a roof. Berengaria succeeded him as queen regnant of Castile.
Berengaria resigned in favor of her son Ferdinand III the Saint of Castile.
The Almohad caliph Yusuf II, Almohad caliph was gored to death while playing with his pet cows, leaving no heir.
The Almohad governor of Andalusia took the majority of his forces across the Strait of Gibraltar to contest the succession to the caliphate.
An Abdallah al-Bayyasi established the Taifa of Baeza with himself at its head and appealed to Ferdinand the Saint to help him conquer Andalusia.
Siege of Jaén (1225): Castile and Baeza failed to take the city of Jaén, Spain.
Ferdinand the Saint established al-Bayyasi at Córdoba, Spain in exchange for Baños de la Encina, Capilla, Badajoz and Salvatierra Castle.
Al-Bayyasi was killed in Córdoba, Spain in a popular uprising. Castile annexed some of his territory including Baeza.
Conquest of Majorca: James the Conqueror led a fleet of some two hundred vessels and twenty thousand men from Salou, Cambrils and Tarragona to Majorca.
Battle of Portopí: Aragonese forces defeated an Almohad force in the Serra de Na Burguesa, forcing the latter to retreat to Palma, Majorca.
Conquest of Majorca: James the Conqueror took the last redoubt of the Almohad forces at Palma, Majorca and captured the vali Abu Yahya.

James the Conqueror issued the Llibre del Repartiment (Majorca), granting territory in Majorca according to participation in its conquest. Half became crown lands; the rest was divided primarily between Catalan and Marseillais knights and the Knights Templar.
Siege of Jaén (1230): Ferdinand the Saint laid siege to Jaén, Spain.
Alfonso IX died. He was succeeded as king of León by his son Ferdinand the Saint.
Siege of Jaén (1230): On hearing of the death of Alfonso IX, Ferdinand the Saint abandoned his siege of Jaén, Spain to be crowned king of León in León, Spain.
Ferdinand the Saint conquered Cazorla.
Battle of Jerez: A Castilian army defeated an army of the emir Ibn Hud near modern Jerez de la Frontera, deep in the latter's territory.
James the Conqueror conquered Menorca.
Ferdinand the Saint conquered Úbeda.
Siege of Burriana: James the Conqueror laid siege to Borriana, Castellón.
Siege of Burriana: The city fell.
James the Conqueror conquered Ibiza.
Siege of Córdoba (1236): Ferdinand the Saint arrived in Córdoba, Spain following its fall at the hands of local knights and internal fifth columnists.
Battle of the Puig: The Valencian king Zayyan ibn Mardanish met an Aragonese invasion force at El Puig, where he was decisively defeated.
Ferdinand the Saint conquered Huelva and obtained the vassalage of Niebla, Andalusia.
James the Conqueror captured Valencia and created himself king of the Kingdom of Valencia.
Ferdinand the Saint conquered Écija and Lucena, Córdoba.
Ferdinand the Saint captured Orihuela and obtained the vassalage of Murcia.
James the Conqueror signed the Treaty of Almizra, establishing Valencia's border with Castile.
Ferdinand the Saint conquered Arjona, Spain, Mula, Spain and Lorca, Spain.
Ferdinand the Saint conquered Cartagena, Spain.
Siege of Jaén (1245–46): Ferdinand the Saint, joined by the Order of Santiago, laid siege to Jaén, Spain.
Siege of Jaén (1245–46): Muhammad I of Granada, king of Granada, surrendered the city to Castile and agreed to tributary relationship. He was created king of the Kingdom of Jaén.
Siege of Seville: Ferdinand the Saint laid siege to Seville.
Ferdinand the Saint obtained the vassalage of Alicante.

Siege of Seville: Seville, the last Muslim polity on the Iberian Peninsula apart from the Emirate of Granada, surrendered to Castile, promising that the city would be turned over no later than the following month. Ferdinand the Saint created himself king of the Kingdom of Seville.
Ferdinand the Saint died. He was succeeded by his son Alfonso X the Wise of Castile.
Alfonso the Wise captured the Algarve from Portugal.
Alfonso the Wise gave his daughter Beatrice of Castile to the Portuguese king Afonso III of Portugal, and promised to cede the Algarve to their firstborn son on his seventh birthday.
King of the Romans William II of Holland was killed in battle with the Frisians near Hoogwoud.
Imperial election, January 1257: Richard, 1st Earl of Cornwall, count of Poitou and earl of Cornwall, was elected King of the Romans.
Imperial election, April 1257: Alfonso the Wise, who claimed the title through descent from his grandfather Philip of Swabia, was elected King of the Romans.
Alfonso the Wise debased the Castilian coinage and introduced a tariff to raise money for a campaign in support of his claim to the rule of the Holy Roman Empire, against that of Richard.
Siege of Jerez (1261): Castile and Granada laid siege to Jerez de la Frontera.
Siege of Jerez (1261): The citizens of Jerez de la Frontera agreed to resume tribute payments to Castile.
James the Conqueror created the Kingdom of Majorca in his will.
Niebla, Andalusia was incorporated into Castile.
Mudéjar revolt of 1264–1266: The Muslim subjects of Castile, encouraged by Muhammad I, rebelled in Andalusia and Murcia.
Mudéjar revolt of 1264–1266: Nuño González de Lara, head of the Castilian garrison at Jerez de la Frontera, fled his post. The Alcázar of Jerez de la Frontera was taken.
Mudéjar revolt of 1264–1266: Castilian forces retook Jerez de la Frontera.
The Siete Partidas, a code of law, was completed in Castile.
Conquest of Murcia (1265–66): James the Conqueror entered Muslim-held territory in support of the Castilian suppression of the Mudéjar revolt.
Conquest of Murcia (1265–66): James the Conqueror laid siege to Murcia.
Conquest of Murcia (1265–66): Murcia surrendered.
Battle of Benevento: Manfred, King of Sicily, the king of Sicily, was killed during the conquest of the kingdom by Charles I of Anjou, count of Anjou.
Alicante was incorporated into Castile.
Alfonso the Wise and Afonso III signed the Treaty of Badajoz, a pact of friendship and mutual assistance. The treaty established the border between Castile and Portugal to the latter's disadvantage.
The Castilian nobility rebelled against Alfonso the Wise following his mismanagement of the economy.
Battle of Écija (1275): Granadan forces routed a Castilian army moving through their territory to meet a Marinid advance.
James the Conqueror died. He was succeeded as king of Aragon and Valencia and count of Barcelona by one son, Peter III the Great of Aragon, and as king of Majorca by another, James II of Majorca.
Siege of Algeciras (1278–79): Castile laid siege to the Marinid port city of Algeciras.
Battle of Algeciras (1278): A combined Marinid-Granadan fleet destroyed the Castilian navy in the Strait of Gibraltar.
James II agreed by treaty to become a vassal of Aragon.
Siege of Algeciras (1278–79): A Marinid force destroyed the Castilian navy in port in the Bay of Gibraltar and captured and executed the soldiers besieging the city.
Battle of Moclín (1280): A force consisting of Castilian soldiers and most of the Order of Santiago was wiped out by a Granadan army at Moclín while returning from a raid.
Alfonso the Wise, facing military pressure from his nobility, was forced to accept his son Sancho IV the Brave of Castile as his heir.
Sicilian Vespers: A number of French officers were killed by locals in rioting near Palermo.

War of the Sicilian Vespers: Sicilian rebels appealed to Peter the Great to overthrow Charles of Anjou's administration and rule by right of his wife Constance of Sicily, Queen of Aragon, Manfred's daughter.
Battle of Malta: An Aragonese fleet surprised and sank a Neapolitan fleet in the Grand Harbour, delaying the latter's planned invasion of Sicily.
Aragonese Crusade: The pope Pope Martin IV called for a crusade against Peter the Great, and declared him deposed in Aragon in favor of Charles, Count of Valois, the count of Valois.
Alfonso the Wise died. He was succeeded by Sancho the Brave, though his will appointed his grandson Alfonso de la Cerda his successor in León.
Battle of the Gulf of Naples: The Aragonese and Sicilian navies drew out a Neapolitan fleet in the Gulf of Naples and captured Charles of Anjou as well as some ten galleys.
Battle of Les Formigues: A Sicilian-Aragonese fleet decisively defeated the French and Genoans, probably near the Formigues Islands.
Battle of the Col de Panissars: An Aragonese force massacred the French army during its retreat over the Pyrenees.

Peter the Great died at Vilafranca del Penedès. He was succeeded as king of Aragon by his eldest son Alfonso III the Liberal, the Free of Aragon and as king of Sicily by his second son James II the Just of Aragon.
Alfonso the Liberal conquered Mallorca.
Alfonso the Liberal conquered Ibiza.
Alfonso the Liberal conquered Menorca and annexed it to the Kingdom of Majorca, dissolving its autonomous government.
Battle of the Counts: A Sicilian-Aragonese fleet defeated a superior Angevin force at Naples, breaking the latter's attempted invasion of Sicily.

The Union of Aragon, a political organization of nobles and townspeople in Aragon, won the Privilege of the Union, a devolution of many royal powers to the Aragonese nobility, from Alfonso the Liberal.
Alfonso the Liberal released Alfonso de la Cerda from captivity in the fortress at Xàtiva and declared him king of Castile and León.

Aragonese Crusade: The pope Pope Nicholas IV, Philip IV the Fair, the Iron King of France, king of France, Charles II the Lame of Naples, king of Naples, and Alfonso the Liberal signed the Treaty of Tarascon, ending the crusade. Alfonso the Liberal agreed to remove all Aragonese troops from Sicily. In return, the pope recognized him as king of Aragon and lifted his excommunication.
Alfonso the Liberal died. He was succeeded by James the Just.
Battle of Iznalloz: The Emirate of Granada expelled a Castillian garrison and the Order of Calatrava from their fortress overlooking the border at Iznalloz.

Sancho the Brave died of tuberculosis in Toledo, Spain. He was succeeded by his young son Ferdinand IV the Summoned of Castile as king of Castile and León, with his wife María de Molina acting as regent.

The pope Pope Boniface VIII, James the Just, Philip the Fair, Charles the Lame and James II of Majorca signed the Treaty of Anagni. Under the treaty, James the Just granted Sicily to the pope, who in turn gifted it to Charles the Lame, and agreed to aid the latter in its reconquest.
War of the Sicilian Vespers: The people of Sicily rejected the Treaty of Anagni and acclaimed James the Just's younger brother Frederick III of Sicily their king.
Aragonese troops invaded Castile in support of Alfonso de la Cerda's claim to the throne.
John of Castile, Lord of Valencia de Campos, a son of Alfonso the Wise, was crowned king of León, Seville and Galicia in León, Spain.
Alfonso de la Cerda was crowned king of Castile, Toledo, Córdoba, Murcia and Jaén at Sahagún.

María de Molina and Denis of Portugal, king of Portugal signed the Treaty of Alcañices. Denis agreed to support Ferdinand the Summoned against the rebels Alfonso de la Cerda and John of Castile and to give him the hand of his daughter Constance of Portugal in marriage. In exchange, he received some Castilian territory along the Portuguese border.
Battle of Cape Orlando: An Aragonese-Angevin fleet defeated the Sicilian navy near Sicily.

Battle of Falconaria: A Sicilian fleet decisively defeated the Neapolitan navy off the shore between Marsala and Trapani and captured its commander, Charles the Lame's son Philip I, Prince of Taranto.
Battle of Ponza (1300): An Aragonese-Angevin fleet defeated a Sicilian one near Ponza.
John of Castile renounced his royal titles and declared his fealty to Ferdinand the Summoned.
In the city of Alicante, Moorish forces attempted a siege.
The Treaty of Madrid was signed in Madrid.
A civil war was started against Enrique de Trastamara, son of Alfonso XI.
Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon were married, laying the foundation for the unification of the kingdoms of Castile and Aragon into Spain.
The reign of Isabella began.
The War of the Castilian Succession began. Vasco Nunez de Balboa was born.
The Spanish Inquisition was founded.
War of the Castilian Succession: The war ended.
The reign of Ferdinand began, marking the foundation of the Kingdom of Spain.
By the Treaty of Alcáçovas, Portugal recognized Spanish control of the Canary Islands.
Spanish conquerors discover (encounter) America
The Reconquista ended.
Jews were expelled from Spain by the Alhambra Decree.
Columbus sets sail.
Spanish colonization of the Americas began.
The Treaty of Tordesillas was signed.
Italian War of 1499–1504: Ferdinand allied with the French King Louis XII of France.
The Rebellion of the Alpujarras (1499–1501), a series of uprisings by the Muslim population of the Kingdom of Granada against their Catholic rulers was defeated.
Isabella I of Castile died. Her daughter, Joanna of Castile succeeded her with her father, Ferdinand as regent
Christopher Columbus died at the age of 51 from an illness.
Spanish conquest of Iberian Navarre began.
Ferdinand died.
Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, became King of Castile and Aragon.
Vasco Nunez de Balboa died.
New Spain began till 1821.
English Queen Mary I of England married Spanish Prince Philip.
Charles abdicated in favor of Philip, who became King Philip II of Spain.
Battle of St. Quentin (1557): Spain won the battle.
Philip moved his court to Madrid.
Dutch Revolt: A revolt began against Habsburg control of the Netherlands. This started the Eighty Years' War
Battle of Lepanto (1571): The Holy League was victorious.
Dutch Revolt: The revolt ended.
The Iberian Union of the crowns of Aragon, Castile and Portugal was established.
Dutch Republic, the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands, declared their independence against Spanish rule.
Anglo–Spanish War (1585): The war began. It was an intermittent conflict
The Spanish Armada was defeated in the English Channel.
The English Armada (known as the Counter Armada) was defeated.
Philip II died in El Escorial, near Madrid, of cancer. He was succeeded by his 20-year-old son, Philip III.
Anglo-Spanish War (1585): The war ends with the treaty of London, which is beneficial to both the Spanish and the English side.
The Treaty of London (1604) was signed concluding the nineteen-year Anglo-Spanish War on peace terms.
The Expulsion of the Moriscos was decreed. The Moriscos were descendants of Spain's Muslim population that had converted to Christianity in the early 16th century.
Thirty Years' War: The war, one of the most destructive conflicts in human history, began.
Philip IV of Spain was crowned.
Portuguese Restoration War: The war began.
The Iberian Union was dissolved.

The Treaty of Westphalia was signed. Habsburg supremacy was curtailed. Recognition of the independence of the Dutch Republic by the Spanish Empire. Recognition of Spanish sovereignty of Southern Netherlands and Luxembourg by the Dutch Republic.
The Peace of the Pyrenees was signed to end the 1635–1659 war between France and Spain. Spain lost French Flanders and northern part of the Principality of Catalonia.
Philip IV died. The Spanish Empire had reached approximately 12.2 million square kilometers (4.7 million square miles) in area
The Treaty of Lisbon was signed. Spain recognized the sovereignty of Portugal's new ruling dynasty, the House of Braganza.
Charles II of Spain, the last Habsburg ruler of the Spanish Empire, was crowned.
Charles II died childless .
House of Bourbon began with Philip V.
War of the Spanish Succession: The war began.
Nueva Planta decrees: Kingdom of Spain as an absolute monarchy and a centralized state, abolishing the political differences of the two crowns (Crown of Castile, Crown of Aragon).
Peace of Utrecht till 1715. The Kingdom of Spain lost Spanish Netherlands, Spanish viceroyalty of Naples and Sicily, Duchy of Milan, Menorca and Gibraltar.
Viceroyalty of New Granada began.
Seven Years' War: Spain declared war on Great Britain.
Treaty of Paris. Spain recovers Florida and obtains Louisiana till 1801.
American Revolutionary War: Spain supported the United States.
Spain during this time opened up the slave trade to Havana.
Spanish base in Nootka Sound. Maximum extension of the Spanish Empire.
Louisiana given to France
British invasions of the Río de la Plata: The invasions began.
British invasions of the Río de la Plata: The invasions ended.
Peninsular War: The war began.
Dos de Mayo Uprising: An uprising took place in Madrid against the French occupation of the city.
Bolivian Independence War: The war began.
Venezuelan War of Independence: The war began.
The Spanish Constitution of 1812 was issued.
Peninsular War: The war ended.
Spanish reconquest of New Granada: The reconquest began.
Spanish reconquest of New Granada: The reconquest ended.
Trienio Liberal: The period began.
Trienio Liberal: The period ended.
Bolivian Independence War: The war ended.
First Carlist War: The war began.
First Carlist War: The war ended.
Second Carlist War: The war began.
Second Carlist War: The war ended.
Chincha Islands War: The war began.
Chincha Islands War: The war ended.
Ten Years' War: A war with Cuba began.
Third Carlist War: The war began.
The First Spanish Republic was established.
Spain under the Restoration: The period began.
The First Spanish Republic was disestablished.
Third Carlist War: The war ended.
Ten Years' War: The war ended.
Pablo Iglesias founds the Partido Socialista Obrero Español or PSOE in Casa Labra, a bar from Madrid
Spanish–American War: The war began.
Spanish–American War: The war ended.
Spanish protectorate in Morocco till 1956.
Spain remained neutral throughout World War I.
Rif War: The war began.
Dictatorship of Primo de Rivera till 1930.
Rif War: The war ended.
The Second Spanish Republic was established.
Spain under the Restoration: The period ended.
Spanish Civil War (to 1939)
Francoist Spain: The period began. Spain stays neutral through World War II
Spain and the United States signs the Pact of Madrid.
Spain joins the United Nations.
Spanish miracle: A period of economic growth began.
Spanish miracle: The period ended.
History of Spain (1975–present)
The Green March forced Spain to hand over its last remaining colonial possession, Spanish Sahara, to Morocco.
Francisco Franco died; the monarchy was restored to Juan Carlos I.
Spanish transition to democracy: The transition began.
First democratic election since 1934.
The Spanish Constitution of 1978 was signed by the King.
Spanish society after the democratic transition: A democratic society was established.
1981 Spanish coup attempt: An attempted coup took place.
Spain joins NATO.
Spain joined the European Union.
1992 Summer Olympics: The Summer Olympics were held in Barcelona.
Spain hosts the 1997 Madrid summit.
Judge Baltasar Garzón issued an international arrest warrant for former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet.
Spain joins Economic and Monetary Union of the European Union. Euro is a real currency, and a single monetary policy is introduced under the authority of the ECB.
Fernando Alonso wins the Hungarian Grand Prix, marking him F1's youngest winner.
2004 Madrid train bombings: Madrid train bombings killed one hundred and ninety-one and injured over two thousand. Prime Minister José María Aznar blamed the Basque terrorists ETA.
Aznar's People's Party lost an election after the Partido Social-Obrero Español of José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero promised to withdraw Spanish troops from Iraq.
PADICAT (archive) established.
Fernando Alonso wins the Championship against Kimi Räikkönen in Brazil, marking him F1's youngest world champion.
2006 Madrid–Barajas Airport bombing: A bombing by ETA ended an active ceasefire and peace negotiations.
Moroccan national Jamal Zougam was found guilty of the 2004 train bombings in Madrid.
Garzón was charged with criminal conduct in three cases, causing an international scandal and protests.
Spain won the UEFA European Championship Final, establishing the team as an international soccer power house.
Spain won the FIFA World Cup.
Garzón was granted leave to work as a consultant to the International Criminal Court at The Hague.
Artur Mas defies Spain by calling early elections on independence of the region of Catalonia.
2017 Barcelona attacks: Barcelona, Cambrils, Alcanar and Subirats were attacked by terrorists from Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL).

2017 Catalan independence referendum: An unconstitutional referendum of independence were called by Generalitat de Catalunya, as Parliament of Catalonia approved the Law on the Referendum of Self-determination of Catalonia. In early September the High Court of Justice of Catalonia had issued orders to the police to try to prevent it, including the detention of various persons responsible for its preparation.

Catalan declaration of independence: Catalan unilateral declaration of independence was ratified by Parliament of Catalonia as the results of the referendum were in favor. Spain considers this action illegal and article 155 of the constitution was applied.
Carles Puigdemont flee from Spain to avoid being arrested after his dismissal by Spain, after proclaiming the independence of Catalonia.
Pedro Sánchez is sworn in as Prime Minister after winning a motion of censure.

Trial of Catalonia independence leaders: Takes place over several months, following the 2017 declaration of independence of Catalonia. Nine defendants sentenced to 9 to 13 years in prison on sedition and misuse of public funds charges; three other defendants fined for disobedience. This sparked subsequent protests by independence citizens.

Sánchez II Government: It become the first nationwide coalition government to be formed in Spain since the Second Spanish Republic. The parties were Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and Unidas Podemos.
COVID-19 pandemic starts in Spain with the first confirmated case in La Gomera (Canary Islands). You can view the confirmed cases, recovered and deaths in this link: COVID-19 pandemic in Spain.
Spain hosts the 2022 Madrid Summit.

The Umayyad Emir Abd al-Rahman III, faced with the threat of invasion by the Fatimids, proclaims himself Caliph of Córdoba. Under the reign of Abd al-Rahman III Muslim Al-Andalus reaches its greatest height before its slow decline over the next four centuries.

The Almohads, founded by Ibn Tumart, began as a religious movement to rid Islam of impurities. Most specifically, the Almohades were opposed to anthropomorphisms which had slipped into Iberian Islam. Ibn Tumart's successor, Abd al-Mu'min, turned the movement against non-Muslims, specifically Jews and Christians. Sweeping across North Africa and into Muslim Iberia, the Almohads initiate riots and persecutions of both Muslims and non-Muslims. In some towns Jews and Christians are given the choice of conversion, exile, or death.
Roman General Julius Caesar invades and conquers the lands of the Belgae: Battle of the Sabis; Siege of the Atuatuci
Julius Caesar campaigns unsuccessfully against the coastal tribes of the Morini and Menapii.
Julius Caesar subdues the Morini.
Ambiorix's revolt under Ambiorix and Cativolcus.
Punitive campaigns subdue Nervii and Treveri; exterminate Eburoni.
Julius Caesar completes writing Commentarii de Bello Gallico, his account of his campaigns in Gaul.
Marcus Nonius Gallus suppresses revolt among Treveri.
Augustus creates the province Gallia Belgica.
Probable origins of the city of Tongeren.
Augusta Treverorum becomes a city.
Nero Claudius Drusus, commander in chief of Roman forces in Gallia Belgica, has a series of canals dug in the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt delta.
Probable origins of the city of Aarlen.
Nero Claudius Drusus dies after falling from his horse. Command of Rome's northern armies passes to Tiberius.
Monument honouring Tiberius erected in Bagacum.
Germanicus becomes commander of the Roman army of the Rhine.
Roman invasion of Germany under command of Germanicus launched from Fectio in Gallia Belgica.
Death of Germanicus.
Treveri revolt at high taxes.
Galba becomes commander of the armies in Lower Germany.
Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo becomes commander of the armies in Lower Germany. Orders canals dug in the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt delta.
Roman law replaces customary law in Gallia Belgica; druids outlawed; Gaulish aristocracy given senatorial rank.
Armies of the Rhine proclaim Aulus Vitellius as emperor.
Treveri, Menapii, Nervii and Tungrii come out in support of the Batavian Revolt, some under compulsion.
Pliny the Elder starts writing his Historia Naturalis, book 4 of which contains a description of Gallia Belgica.
Northern border fortified with series of castra.
Domitian restructures provinces of the Roman Empire: Gallia Belgica divided into the provinces of Belgica Prima, Belgica Secunda, Germania Superior and Germania Inferior.
Chauci launch maritime raids on the coasts of Gallia Belgica.
Carausius, a Menapian general in the Roman army, declares himself emperor of Britain and Gaul.
Death of Carausius, brings the end of the Carausian revolt 3 years later.
Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, attends the Council of Serdica.
Land south of the Rhine delta ceded to Frankish foederati
Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, attends the Council of Ariminum.
Salian Franks take possession of Tournai.
Childeric I buried in Tournai.
Sigebert I inherits the Frankish kingdom of Austrasia.
Death of Gertrude of Nivelles
Death of Amandus.
Murder of Dagobert II in the Ardennes Forest.
Pepin of Herstal and his wife Plectrude found what will become the Abbey of Saint-Hubert.
Death of Begga.
Death of Lambert of Maastricht: murdered at a site that would become Liège.
See of Maastricht moved to the location of Lambert of Maastricht's murder, now Liège.
Death of Hubertus, Bishop of Liège.
Birth of Charlemagne, first Holy Roman Emperor.
Louis the Pious confirms the liberties granted to St Bavo's Abbey by Charlemagne (oldest extant original charter in a Belgian archive).
First recorded Viking raid on the Flemish coast.
The remains of St Hubert (died 727) installed in the monastery that would become the Abbey of Saint-Hubert.

Treaty of Verdun divides the Carolingian Empire between the three sons of Louis the Pious: Lothair I, Louis the German and Charles the Bald, creating the kingdom of Middle Francia (including most of the Low Countries) for Lothair and assigning Flanders to Charles the Bald.
Norsemen raid Flanders.
Treaty of Prüm divides Middle Francia into the Kingdom of Lotharingia (including most of the Low Countries), the Kingdom of Provence and the Kingdom of Italy.
Treaty of Meerssen partitions Lotharingia (including most of the Low Countries) between East Francia (Germany) and West Francia (France).
Norsemen raid Taxandria.
Norsemen raid Tournaisis.
Norsemen plunder Cambrai and encamp near Maastricht, extorting tribute from Maastricht, Tongeren, Liège, Sint-Truiden, Malmedy, Stavelot, and Prüm.
Norse invaders defeated in Battle on the Dijle.
Holy Roman Emperor Arnulf of Carinthia appoints his illegitimate son Zwentibold as king of Lotharingia.
Zwentibold slain by Count Reginar I of Hainault; Lotharingia reincorporated into East Francia.
Bishop of Liège granted right to levy a toll in Maastricht.
Count Reginar I of Hainault appointed margrave of Lotharingia; historically regarded as the first Duke of Lorraine.
Death of Reginar, Duke of Lorraine, at his palace in Meerssen; succeeded by his son Giselbert.
Death of Baldwin II, Margrave of Flanders at Blandijnberg; succeeded by his son Arnulf.
Henry the Fowler invades Lotharingia and receives oaths of loyalty from the local aristocracy.
Gilbert, Duke of Lorraine, attends the coronation of Otto I in Aachen.
Battle of Andernach: death of Gilbert, Duke of Lorraine; end of independence of Lotharingia (referred to as "Belgica" in the 10th-century histories of Richer of Rheims).
Saint-Ghislain Abbey reformed by Gérard of Brogne
Death of Isaac, Count of Cambrai; powers of count transferred to Fulbert, Bishop of Cambrai.
Bruno the Great, Archbishop of Cologne, appointed Duke of Lotharingia.
Hungarian attackers raid Lower Lotharingia, besiege Cambrai.
Bruno the Great divides Lotharingia into Upper Lotharingia (the later Duchy of Lorraine) and Lower Lotharingia (the later Duchy of Lothier).
Death of Gérard of Brogne.
Godfrey I, Duke of Lower Lorraine, dies in Italy; no immediate successor.
Death of Arnulf I, Count of Flanders; succession of Arnulf II, Count of Flanders
Otto I, Holy Roman Emperor, confirms Godfrey of Lower Lotharingia's gift to Saint-Ghislain Abbey of 18 mansi of land in Villers-Saint-Ghislain.
Death of Bruno the Great, Duke of Lotharingia.
Lothar, King of the Franks, confirms the possessions of St. Peter's Abbey, Ghent, including those bequeathed by Arnulf I, Count of Flanders, and contested by his heirs.
Richar, Count of Mons, appointed Duke of Lower Lotharingia.
Richar, Duke of Lower Lotharingia, dies; no immediate successor.
Otto II, Holy Roman Emperor, appoints Charles, brother of Lothair of France, as Duke of Lower Lotharingia.

Otto II, Holy Roman Emperor, confirms all previous endowments to Notker, Bishop of Liège, and issues a general immunity for the bishopric's lands: beginning of the establishment of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège.
Otto III, King of Germany, endows Notker, Bishop of Liège, with the County of Huy: full establishment of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège.
Death of Arnulf II, Count of Flanders; succession of Baldwin IV, Count of Flanders.
Death of Hildegard of Flanders, daughter of Arnulf II, Count of Flanders, and wife of Dirk II, Count of Holland.
Baldrick II succeeds Notger as prince-bishop of Liège

Battle of Vlaardingen: imperial forces commanded by Godfrey II, Duke of Lower Lorraine, and Baldrick II, bishop of Liège, defeated by the army of Dirk III, Count of Holland. Baldrick died after a sudden illness on the journey; Godfrey was captured in the battle.
Wolbodo consecrated bishop of Liège.
Durandus succeeds Wolbodo as prince-bishop of Liège
Reginard succeeds Durandus as prince-bishop of Liège
Death of Baldwin IV, Count of Flanders; succession of Baldwin V, Count of Flanders
Nithard succeeds Reginard as prince-bishop of Liège
Wazo succeeds Nithard as prince-bishop of Liège
Baldwin V, Count of Flanders, seizes control of the imperial castle at Ename
Theodwin succeeds Wazo as prince-bishop of Liège
Forces of Theodwin of Liège defeat forces of Dirk IV, Count of Holland, killing Dirk and restoring imperial authority in the Rhine delta.
Baldwin V, Count of Flanders, becomes regent of France
Ename Abbey founded
Theodwin of Liège grants city rights to Huy, the oldest such charter to survive from what is now Belgium.
Death of Baldwin V, Count of Flanders; succession of Baldwin VI, Count of Flanders
Genealogia comitum Flandrensium compiled.
Death of Baldwin VI, Count of Flanders; succession of Arnulf III, Count of Flanders
Battle of Cassel between Robert the Frisian and his nephew, Arnulf III, Count of Flanders. Arnulf was killed in the battle and Robert succeeded him as count.
Pope Gregory VII issues bull of protection for the Abbey of Saint-Hubert.
Pope Gregory VII writes to Theodwin, bishop of Liège, urging him to leave the abbot of Saint-Hubert unmolested.
Death of Theodwin of Liège.
Pope Gregory VII issues bull of protection for Watten Abbey.
Adela of Flanders marries Canute IV of Denmark
Traditional date of the first apparition of Our Lady of Tongre.
Adela of Flanders, queen consort of Denmark, returns to the Low Countries after her husband's murder
Godfrey of Bouillon becomes Duke of Lower Lorraine
Death of Robert I, Count of Flanders; succession of Robert II, Count of Flanders
Godfrey of Bouillon, Duke of Lower Lorraine, sets off as one of the leaders of the First Crusade.
Death of Godfrey of Bouillon
Baldric of Noyon, Bishop of Tournai, awards the right of presentment for Tielt to the chapter of St Salvator in Harelbeke.
St Michael's church, Hekelgem becomes a dependency of Affligem Abbey.
Godfrey I, Count of Louvain, invested as Duke of Lower Lotharingia in Worms Cathedral.
The hermit Ligerius founds a community that would become Ten Duinen Abbey (the Abbey of Dunes).
Death of Robert II, Count of Flanders; succession of Baldwin VII, Count of Flanders
Death of Baldwin VII, Count of Flanders; succession of Charles I, Count of Flanders (Charles the Good)
Godfrey I, Count of Louvain confirms the agreement of Ava of Waver and her sons with the priory of Forest, transferring ownership of an allod in Woluwe.
Murder of Charles the Good, Count of Flanders
Albero I of Louvain, prince-bishop of Liège, dies; succeeded by Alexander of Jülich
Foundation of Park Abbey.
Godfrey I, Count of Louvain, dies; succeeded by Godfrey II
Siege of Bouillon Castle by Albero, prince-bishop of Liège.
Godfrey II, Count of Louvain dies; succeeded by Godfrey III
Pope Eugene III confirms Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot and Malmedy, in possession of the goods of the abbey.
Henry II of Leez, Bishop of Liège, confirms Affligem Abbey in possession of its property in the diocese of Liège.
Godfrey III, Count of Louvain, takes Grimbergen

Henry the Blind, Count of Namur and of Luxembourg, being childless, names his sister Alice of Namur with her husband Baldwin IV, Count of Hainaut, and their son Baldwin, as heirs of all his allodial possessions, "with sod and twig", retaining usufruct during his own lifetime.
Henry II of Leez, prince-bishop of Liège, dies
Rudolf of Zähringen becomes prince-bishop of Liège
Death of Thierry, Count of Flanders; succession of Philip of Alsace as count of Flanders
Baldwin IV, Count of Hainaut, dies; succeeded by Baldwin V
Gislebert of Mons becomes chancellor to Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut.
Godfrey III, Count of Louvain, departs for Jerusalem

Henry the Blind, Count of Namur and of Luxembourg, being childless, names his nephew, Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut, already heir to all his allodial possessions, as heir equally to all his feudal possessions, "with sod and twig", retaining usufruct during his own lifetime.
Saint Lambert's Cathedral, Liège, destroyed by fire.
birth of Ermesinde, later countess of Luxembourg, only child of Henry the Blind. As a female heir she would inherit his allodial possessions, but not his feudal possessions.
Godfrey III, Count of Louvain dies; succeeded by Henry I, Duke of Brabant
Death of Philip of Alsace, Count of Flanders; succession of his daughter Margaret I, Countess of Flanders, and her husband and co-ruler Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut
Murder of Albert of Louvain, prince-bishop of Liège, by supporters of Emperor Henry VI
Relics of Saint Alena enshrined in Forest Priory.
Peace treaty between Henry I, Duke of Brabant and Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut, ending twelve years of conflict between the Duchy of Brabant and the County of Hainaut.
Death of Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut; succession of his son Baldwin VI as count of Flanders and Hainaut
Henry I, Duke of Brabant, departs for Jerusalem.
Baldwin VI, Count of Hainaut, donates all his possessions in the village of Horrues to the collegiate church of Soignies to endow a Lady chapel and a chantry.
Battle of Adrianople: Baldwin I of Constantinople, count of Flanders and Hainaut, captured by the Bulgarians
Henry I, Duke of Brabant, marries Marie of France in Soissons.
Battle of Bouvines: decisive French victory against the forces of Ferdinand, Count of Flanders, Henry I, Duke of Brabant, and Otto IV, Holy Roman Emperor. Count of Flanders carried captive to Paris.

Guy of Saint-Pol and his brother, Hugo of Saint-Pol, stand surety for a loan of 3693 pounds borrowed from citizens of Arras by Daniel, Lord of Béthune: an early example of the use of French rather than Latin in legal documents.
Henry I, Duke of Brabant, issues charter of city rights for Brussels.
Ferdinand, Count of Flanders and Joan, Countess of Flanders release inhabitants of the Brugse Vrije from the feudal relief of "best beast".
Henry I, Duke of Brabant, died; succeeded by Henry II
Statutes of the Ghent Leper Hospital translated from Latin: the earliest known example of a legal document entirely in Dutch.
Charters of the city of Ghent translated into Dutch.
Benedictine priory at Vorst, a dependency of Affligem Abbey, becomes the independent Forest Abbey.
Pope Innocent IV authorizes the canons regular of St Augustine to establish a grammar school in Leuven.
Henry II, Duke of Brabant, died; succeeded by Henry III
Gothic choir of Tournai Cathedral completed
Henry III, Duke of Brabant, dies; succeeded by Henry IV

Margaret of Constantinople, Countess of Flanders, impounds wares of English merchants in Flanders in retaliation for their king's non-payment of a money fief, sparking a trade war between Flanders and England.
Henry IV, Duke of Brabant, died; succeeded by John I
Treaty of Montreuil-sur-Mer between Edward I of England and Guy, Count of Flanders, ending four years of economic warfare and providing for free movement of merchants between their territories.
Future John II, Duke of Brabant, born.

Guy de Thourout does homage to Guy, Count of Flanders for lands in Wervik, Reninge and Rollegem. He also held land in Menen and Rekkem, a manor in Varsenare, and owned a number of houses within the city of Ypres.
Battle of Worringen
Aldermen of Nieuwpoort accept the mediation of Guy, Count of Flanders in their dispute with the abbeys of Duinen and Bourbourg concerning a dyke built near the town.
John I, Duke of Brabant, died; succeeded by John II
John II, Duke of Brabant, recognises that Affligem Abbey by immemorial custom has the right to appoint a panel of seven aldermen for the village of Hekelgem.
Edward I of England grants Flemish merchants the right to buy wool for export anywhere in the British Isles, rather than being limited to the wool staple.
Treaties of alliance between Philip IV of France and John of Avesnes, Count of Hainaut, culminate in a trade treaty allowing merchants from Hainaut to trade freely in the kingdom of France.
Battle of the Golden Spurs: Flemish forces defeat knights of Philip IV of France near Kortrijk
Aldermen of the city of Namur authorize formation of a butchers' guild with militia obligations, requiring members to arm themselves, follow their own banner, and bury their own dead.

The Charter of Kortenberg finalised at Kortenberg Abbey, establishing fundamental rights for the inhabitants of the Duchy of Brabant such as no punishment without due process. Council of four knights and ten representatives of the boroughs established (beginnings of representative institutions in the duchy).
Henry of Luxembourg died in Buonconvento while besieging Siena, reputedly of poison put in the chalice during mass.
Works begins on a new cloth hall in Leuven, which is now University Hall.
Joanna of Brabant born.
Rebellion of the commoners in maritime Flanders, sparked by Louis I, Count of Flanders, ceding Sluis to John I, Marquis of Namur.
Pope John XXII provides a dispensation for the marriage of Philippa of Hainault and Edward III of England. The marriage itself took place by proxy in Valenciennes in October.
Marriage of Philippa of Hainault and Edward III of England celebrated in York Minster.
Battle of Cassel: Philip VI of France defeats Flemish rebels led by Nicolaas Zannekin.

Treaty of mutual support between John III, Duke of Brabant and Louis I, Count of Flanders, and the cities subject to them, providing for offensive and defensive alliance and free trade between their territories.
Battle of Sluys
Jacob van Artevelde killed in Ghent.

The boroughs of the Duchy of Brabant and the Duchy of Limburg undertake to remain united under a single prince after the death of John III, Duke of Brabant, not allowing the territory to be divided among his heirs.
Joyous Entry of 1356: Joanna, Duchess of Brabant and her husband Wenceslaus I of Luxembourg sign the great charter of liberties of the Duchy of Brabant.
Extirpation of small Jewish population of Brabant after accusations of profaning eucharistic hosts.
Ghent Revolt led by Philip van Artevelde begins
Battle of Beverhoutsveld – men of Ghent take Bruges and gain control over most of the county of Flanders
Battle of Dunkirk

Louis II, Count of Flanders, last count of the House of Dampierre, dies; succeeded by his daughter Margaret III, Countess of Flanders, whose husband Philip the Bold ruled on her behalf: beginning of period of Burgundian rule in the Low Countries
Peace of Tournai ends the Ghent Revolt
Philip the Bold founds the Lille Chamber of Accounts to audit the accounts of his functionaries in the county of Flanders.
Oldest record of the incorporation of the Brussels guild of painters, goldbeaters and glassmakers.
John of Bavaria elected Prince-Bishop of Liège (resigned 1418).
Joanna, Duchess of Brabant secretly relinquishes possession of the Duchy of Brabant to her niece, Margaret of Male, and offspring thereof.
John of Bavaria, bishop-elect of Liège, writes to Philip the Bold to intercede for merchants from Liège arrested by the officers of Rethel.
John the Fearless takes fiscal measures to pay Alexander Stewart, Earl of Mar's archers joining him on the Liège campaign. (Letter bearing only known surviving signature of John the Fearless).
Suppression of the Homines Intelligentiae in Brussels.
Philip the Good transfers usufruct of the County of Namur to John of Flanders, Lord of Béthune, for the duration of his life.
Pope Martin V issues papal bull founding University of Leuven.
Tapestry weavers of Oudenaarde form the Guild of St Barbara.
Tournament held on the main square in Leuven in the presence of Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy and Brabant.
Guilds of Ghent take up arms against the Count of Flanders, Philip the Good.
Philip the Good declares war on the city of Ghent.
Battle of Gavere: forces of Philip the Good defeat rebels of Ghent, ending their rebellion.
The Feast of the Pheasant, a banquet given by Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, held in Lille.
Tower of St. Peter's Church, Leuven, catches fire.
Estates General of 1464: first joint meeting of representatives of various territories of the Burgundian Netherlands.
Battle of Montenaken: forces of Philip the Good defeat Liège militiamen.
Dinant sacked by the forces of Philip the Good, commanded by Charles the Bold
Death of Philip the Good; Charles the Bold succeeds as Duke of Burgundy.
Marriage of Charles the Bold and Margaret of York (Now commemorated with the five-yearly Procession of the Golden Tree)
Charles the Bold grants Prince-Bishop Louis of Bourbon permission to begin rebuilding Liège.
Charles the Bold appointed mediator in the peace negotiations between Poland and Hungary.
Charles the Bold dies in the Battle of Nancy.
Birth of Philip the Fair
Battle of Guinegate: forces of Mary of Burgundy and her husband Maximilian I of Habsburg defeat forces of Louis XI of France.
Birth of Margaret of Burgundy

Mary of Burgundy dies as a result of having fallen from her horse while hawking some weeks earlier. Leaving an infant heir and a foreign husband, this set the scene for the Flemish revolts against Maximilian of Austria (1483–1485).
Treaty of Senlis: Charles VIII of France cedes the County of Flanders and County of Artois to the House of Habsburg.
Wedding contracts concluded for the double marriage of Philip the Fair and Margaret of Burgundy to Joanna of Castile and John, Prince of Asturias.
Henry of Bergen, Bishop of Cambrai, celebrates nuptial mass of Philip the Handsome and Joanna of Castile at St Gummarus Church, Lier.
Birth of the future Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, in Ghent.
Birth of Isabella of Austria, daughter of Philip of Burgundy and Joanna of Castile, future Queen of Christian II of Denmark.
Katherine Hasselet commissioned to produce a series of tapestries on the life of St Anatoile — now the oldest known Flemish tapestries extant
Pope Julius II grants indulgence for those contributing to the rebuilding of the collegiate church of Dinant, equal to the indulgence for a pilgrimage to Rome.
Érard de La Marck, Prince-Bishop of Liège, orders publication of Julius II's bull granting an indulgence for those contributing to the rebuilding of the collegiate church of Dinant.

Charles V issues decree for the Habsburg Netherlands prohibiting Lutheran preaching, teaching, printing or disputation, largely parallel to the Edict of Worms that he was to sign for the Empire as a whole on 26 May but providing more repressive powers to secular authorities.
Johann Esch and Heinrich Voes burned at the stake in Brussels for their adherence to Lutheran doctrines.

Peace of Madrid temporarily ends the war between Charles V and Francis I of France, with France briefly relinquishing all claim to the County of Flanders, County of Artois, Tournai and the Tournaisis, and the Duchy of Burgundy.
Mary of Hungary appointed regent over the Habsburg Netherlands.
Charles V issues decree establishing protocols and procedure of the reorganized Council of Luxembourg.
New edict requiring printers and booksellers to provide local magistrates with inventories of their stock.
University of Leuven issues the first index of prohibited books.
French forces plunder Arlon.
Peace of Crépy ends the war between Charles V and Francis I of France, returning status quo of 1538: Duchy of Luxembourg restored to the Habsburg Netherlands.
Edict regulating the organization of markets throughout the Habsburg Netherlands.
King Philip establishes the Royal Library of the Low Countries.
Compromise of Nobles petition Margaret of Parma to suspend the laws on heresy.
Attempted Calvinist coup in Antwerp.

Duke of Alva banishes thirty inhabitants of the city of Antwerp and their spouses, with forfeiture of property, for supporting or disseminating Calvinism – including the pensionary of the city, Jacques van Wesenbeke, and the head of the Calvinist consistory in Antwerp, the Portuguese merchant Marcus Perez.
Maximilien Morillon founds the first diocesan seminary in Mechelen.
Abraham Ortelius' Theatrum Orbis Terrarum published in Antwerp.
Gerard van Groesbeeck, Prince-Bishop of Liège, promulgates a new codification of the legal procedures in the principality's courts.
Don Luis de Requesens, Governor of the Habsburg Netherlands, issues general pardon to rebels willing to return to loyalty.

Philip II of Spain decrees that the change of year is to be counted from 1 January throughout the Habsburg Netherlands, rather than from Christmas (25 December), the Feast of the Annunciation (25 March) or Easter day, as was the custom in various parts.
Sack of Antwerp by Spanish mutineers from the Army of Flanders.
John of Austria makes his formal entry into Brussels as Governor General of the Low Countries.
Governor General John of Austria dies near Namur.
Union of Arras concluded.
Archduke Albert arrives in Brussels to begin his administration as Governor General of the Habsburg Netherlands.
Army of Flanders takes Amiens.
Peace of Vervins signed.
Edict prohibiting all trade with the enemy issued.
Battle of Lekkerbeetje in the countryside outside 's-Hertogenbosch
Siege of Ostend begins.
General assault on Ostend launched.
Federico Spinola dies in the Battle of Sluis.
Maurice of Nassau lays siege to Sluis.
Don Íñigo de Borja repulses attempted Dutch landing at Blokkersdijk, near Antwerp.
Beginning of a series of six witch trials in Laarne (ending May 1608).
Death of Joannes Bochius, secretary to the city of Antwerp
Perpetual Edict (1611) reforming the basic rules of criminal and civil procedure in the courts of the Habsburg Netherlands.
Aylid, wife of Giele le Hayverlin, sentenced to death for witchcraft by the magistrates of Ouffet: one of the first trials in a local spate of witchcraft accusations.
Fund-raising lottery held to fund the opening of Mounts of piety in the Low Countries.
Opening of Mount of piety (low-interest loan bank) in Brussels, founded by Wenceslas Cobergher.
Tax resistance by Guilds of Brussels.
First Flemish newspaper, Nieuwe Tijdinghen, begins regular publication.
Twelve Years' Truce expires.
Battle of Fleurus: Army of Flanders defeats Protestant German invasion force.
Fr Charles of Brussels preaches the Forty Hours' Devotion at the court chapel in Brussels.
Siege of 's-Hertogenbosch: one of the four chief cities of the Duchy of Brabant falls to the Dutch Republic.
Political crisis: Conspiracy of Nobles and Siege of Maastricht prompt Isabella Clara Eugenia, Governess General of the Spanish Netherlands, to summon the final session of the Estates General.
Death of Isabella Clara Eugenia
Arrival of Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand of Austria as new governor general.
